First find what transition has an energy of about  

E ≃ 3.9 × 10⁻⁶ eV.

Convert this to frequency:

E = hν  ⇒ ν = E/h  
  = (3.9 × 10⁻⁶ eV)(1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹)/(6.626×10⁻³⁴ J s)  
  ≈ 9.4 × 10⁸ Hz  ≈  0.94 GHz.

This corresponds to a wavelength  

λ = c/ν ≃ 0.32 m ≃ 32 cm.

The rest–frame hyperfine (spin–flip) line of neutral atomic hydrogen (H I) is at 21 cm (ν₀ = 1.420 GHz, E₀ ≈ 5.9 μeV).  
An observed energy of 3.9 μeV (or wavelength ≃32 cm) is just the 21-cm line red-shifted by

1 + z = E₀ / E ≃ 5.9 μeV / 3.9 μeV ≃ 1.5  →  z ≃ 0.5,

which is exactly what one expects for a source at ≈2 Gpc.

Thus the line must be the H I 21-cm transition. In the Milky Way, 21-cm absorption is produced almost exclusively by the cold neutral (atomic) medium, because the optical depth varies inversely with the spin temperature; the warm neutral medium is usually too optically thin to yield a strong absorption feature.

Therefore the absorption line is most likely tracing the cold atomic interstellar medium.

Answer: C
